transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), Alicia Torres (Vela VP Eng), Raj Patel (Vela SRE), Maya Chen (Vela Security), Evan Ross (Vela Product)

Summary: quick sync after incident on 2026-03-02; focus on technical root cause, mitigations, and next steps.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I know this is short notice so appreciate you squeezing this in. we'll run through the timeline, what we did, what we're still investigating and actions. Samira is gonna start with tech details.
[00:28] Samira Khan: yeah thanks Jordan. um so quick recap — on Monday 03/02 at ~10:13 UTC we saw a spike in P90/P99 latency for the hosted inference route for the vela-prod account, requests queued up, some timeouts, and we triggered the fallback to the smaller model per the policy.
[01:05] Raj Patel: yep, to confirm for context we had a couple customer-facing pages degrade, about 15% of traffic hit the fallback, error rate increased to ~4% for a 20 minute window.
[01:24] Jordan Lee: thanks Raj. Samira, can you describe the mitigation you pushed?
[01:33] Samira Khan: sure — immediate mitigation was threefold: 1) emergency throttle at rate limit layer to 60 RPS for the heaviest route, 2) force fallback to the smaller model variant for the most latency-sensitive endpoints, and 3) we disabled an aggressive autoscaler burst policy that had been misconfigured — I should say the autoscaler was scaling up but not fast enough due to spot scheduling delays.
[02:05] Alicia Torres: there was a note about kv cache — did the cache get invalidated? some of our engineers saw a big cold-cache effect.
[02:16] Samira Khan: right so our working hypothesis is a cascade: a traffic burst caused many new requests with longer prefixes, the KV cache didn't have high locality for those prefixes which led to lots of cache misses and memory churn, which under certain kernel schedules increased inference latency — folks will see this described in the RCA, but in short KV cache thrash + autoscaler lag.
[02:45] Evan Ross: when you say Kv cache thrash is that the key-value cache inside sessions? could that be exacerbated by certain prompt patterns?
[02:55] Samira Khan: yes it's the per-session KV cache. long context prompts with many unique prefixes reduce locality; replay tests show the same patterns. we also saw the batching window grow which increased tail latency.
[03:20] Raj Patel: quick question — you mentioned batching window, is that because of request shaping or because of the autoscaler?
[03:28] Samira Khan: it's combination: when instances are saturated the runtime extends the batching window to maximize throughput, which helps average cost but hurts tail. during the burst that worsened the P99.
[03:50] Maya Chen: from security/compliance side we noted logs were incomplete for the degraded window; audit logs had a gap of ~6 minutes. any idea why?
[04:02] Priya Nair: yeah we saw that — that looked like an ingestion backlog to the logging pipeline; logs were buffered and then processed after the incident window. we've flagged this with infra.
[04:18] Jordan Lee: to be explicit on impact — the customer-facing SLA triggers we saw were primarily latency and availability hits, not data loss. can the team confirm?
[04:28] Raj Patel: correct, no user data was dropped, all requests either succeeded later or hit fallback.
[04:36] Jordan Lee: ok thanks. next, root cause hypothesis and evidence. Samira?
[04:42] Samira Khan: short version: psuedo-root cause is three things aligning: an unusual traffic spike with low locality, KV cache misses causing memory churn, and autoscaler config that didn't provision fast enough because of node provisioning delay (spot interruption + placement). we have metrics: cache hit ratio dropped from 92% to 43% during the window, queue lengths per instance spiked to >300, and CPU on the instances hit sustained 95%.
[05:18] Alicia Torres: is that 92% number baseline for our workload? seems high.
[05:23] Samira Khan: baseline is 88-93 depending on route, yeah this was an outlier.
[05:28] Evan Ross: one of our concerns — could this happen again if traffic patterns change? what permanent controls can we put in?
[05:36] Samira Khan: absolutely — we recommend three short-to-mid term fixes: 1) conservative throttling windows adjustable per route, 2) KV cache tuning and eviction policy changes for long-prefix workloads, and 3) autoscaler policy changes (faster warm pool, enable reserved capacity for critical routes).
[06:00] Raj Patel: reserved capacity — that costs more, can we get an idea of delta?
[06:07] Jordan Lee: we can send a sizing and cost delta; initial estimate for the reserved pool to cover peak would be ~2.5x current baseline for the critical route which is roughly a 15-20% increase in committed spend — Samira will follow up with bench numbers.
[06:28] Maya Chen: do you have SOC2 docs related to logging and audit retention available — we need to attach to our internal postmortem.
[06:36] Priya Nair: yes Priya here, I'll share the SOC2 pack and the compliance links after this call.
[06:43] Maya Chen: great, thanks.
[07:00] Samira Khan: quick note on the throttling PR — we implemented a staged throttle that is route-aware and can be toggled; it reduces headroom but protects P99. the PR is in our internal repo and we'll push a snapshot with config to you.
[07:20] Alicia Torres: timeline for PR?
[07:24] Jordan Lee: Jordan — we'll share the PR and the benchmark snapshot by Friday 2026-03-06.
[07:31] Alicia Torres: ok.
[08:00] [08:00] Jordan Lee: moving to mitigations applied during incident — Samira you already covered emergency throttle and fallback; anything else?
[08:10] Samira Khan: we also temporarily disabled model quantization fallback attempts that caused extra scheduling work; that had small improvement. we rolled a config that tightened the batching window for the most latency-sensitive endpoints which reduced tail but increased token cost.
[08:35] Evan Ross: cost tradeoffs noted — can you quantify token cost delta when batching window tightened?
[08:42] Samira Khan: initial runs show +6-9% token cost for 30-40% P99 improvement in that route — we'll include numbers in the bench.
[08:58] Raj Patel: about the on-prem pilot — we had previously discussed private deployment; is that still recommended?
[09:05] Jordan Lee: yes for the most sensitive workloads we recommended Private/Dedicated; we can run a constrained pilot so you can validate isolation, KMS integration, and determinism. tentative kickoff week of 2026-03-09.
[09:22] Alicia Torres: our timeline for SLA work is tight — we want to have mitigation in place before end of Q2.
[09:30] Jordan Lee: understood.
[09:40] Samira Khan: digging a bit more into the cache behavior — we saw thrash correlate with prompt pattern changes from a new marketing campaign (different prefixes). suggestion: add adaptive prefix grouping so caching is less sensitive to small changes in prefix tokens.
[10:05] Raj Patel: can you show us traces for a sample user session? we'll scrub PII.
[10:12] Jordan Lee: yes please send sample traces to the case we will open. Raj to share by Thursday.
[10:25] Maya Chen: note — we need artifact proving no key material left on shared hosts; also KMS rotation logs.
[10:33] Priya Nair: noted, we'll surface KMS audit and rotation policy.
[10:40] Jordan Lee: any blockers for the actions?
[10:44] Alicia Torres: only blocker is access to the traces and scheduling the pilot — otherwise sounds good.
[10:50] Jordan Lee: ok moving to timeline and owners recap.
[11:00] Jordan Lee: action item recap: Jordan to send PR & bench (2026-03-06), Samira to run replay with KV cache enabled and share perf numbers (2026-03-05), Raj to provide traces (2026-03-05), Maya to validate KMS docs (2026-03-09), Priya to share SOC2 evidence.
[11:30] Evan Ross: one clarifying q — what about model fallbacks being automatic? we saw some oscillation. can we make fallbacks sticky for a short window?
[11:42] Samira Khan: yes we can implement a sticky fallback TTL per session to avoid oscillation, that is on the backlog now; we'll prioritize if you want.
[12:00] Raj Patel: yes please prioritize the sticky fallback it's useful.
[12:08] Jordan Lee: noted. we'll include backlog priority in the follow-up.
[12:20] Alicia Torres: are you aware of any competitors offering guarantees around this kind of workload pattern?
[12:27] Jordan Lee: some vendors claim better tail SLOs but often at higher cost or with private deployments. folks mentioned Megacloud AI but with higher committed spend; we'll surface a competitive note separately.
[12:45] Priya Nair: closing notes — we'll schedule the pilot kickoff week of 2026-03-09, confirm day next week.
[13:00] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone, appreciate the fast sync. we'll send the notes, PR link, bench numbers and SOC2 pack. any last words?
[13:15] Maya Chen: thanks, please include contact for security follow-up.
[13:22] Jordan Lee: will do.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-generated with a few mis-hearings (KV vs K V, autoscaler sometimes transcribed as auto-scaler). Some speaker labels normalized.
